polytrichum-commune: One of the tallest mosses: stiff, star-tipped stems that can top 30 cm in damp heaths and bogs.
polytrichum-juniperinum: A haircap of dry, sunny ground, with bluish needle-like leaves ending in red-brown points.
sphagnum-palustre: A plump peat moss that holds many times its weight in water and builds bogs over centuries.
sphagnum-capillifolium: A crimson-tinged peat moss that forms firm hummocks on bogs and moorland.
hylocomium-splendens: Adds a new feathery tier every year, stacking up like stairs on northern forest floors.
pleurozium-schreberi: Red stems and glossy feathery shoots that carpet acid woods and heaths across the north.
hypnum-cupressiforme: A very common plait moss weaving flat mats over trunks, rocks, walls and roofs.
dicranum-scoparium: Its leaves all sweep to one side, as if combed by the wind; found on woodland soil and logs.
leucobryum-glaucum: Pale grey-green cushions on forest floors, almost white when dry thanks to hollow water cells.
thuidium-tamariscinum: Finely branched like a tiny fern, three times divided, carpeting damp woodland.
ceratodon-purpureus: A pioneer of pavements, burnt ground and roofs, with capsule stalks that turn purple-red.
funaria-hygrometrica: First to settle on old bonfire sites; its stalks twist as the air dries, hence its name.
bryum-argenteum: Silvery shoots no bigger than a pinhead, thriving in pavement cracks in cities worldwide.
tortula-muralis: Small cushions on old walls, each leaf tipped with a long silvery hair.
grimmia-pulvinata: Hoary grey cushions on walls and roofs, its capsules bent back down into the cushion.
syntrichia-ruralis: Curls up tightly when dry, then opens into a green star within minutes of rain.
kindbergia-praelonga: A delicate feather moss trailing over damp soil, logs and stones in the shade.
brachythecium-rutabulum: A coarse, glossy feather moss of soil, logs and lawns, with rough capsule stalks.
rhytidiadelphus-squarrosus: The moss of damp lawns, its leaves bent sharply outwards like little stars.
rhytidiadelphus-loreus: Loose, untidy shoots with leaves swept one way, on mossy forest floors in wet climates.
atrichum-undulatum: Long wavy leaves that crinkle when dry, on shaded banks and woodland paths.
mnium-hornum: Bright green tufts on acid banks and tree bases, with toothed, translucent leaves.
plagiomnium-undulatum: Its shoots look like tiny palm trees, with long wavy leaves, in damp woods.
plagiomnium-affine: A thyme moss with broad toothed leaves on arching stems, in damp woods and grassland.
fissidens-taxifolius: Leaves in two flat rows like a yew sprig, each folded into a small pocket at its base.
climacium-dendroides: A miniature tree: an upright stem crowned with branches, in wet meadows and fens.
fontinalis-antipyretica: Trails in streams; its name means against fire, as it was packed around chimneys.
homalothecium-sericeum: Silky golden-green mats on walls and trunks, its branches curling up when dry.
pseudoscleropodium-purum: Plump, neat shoots with rounded overlapping leaves, frequent in grassland and heath.
leucodon-sciuroides: Curved branches that look like squirrel tails, on tree trunks and old walls.
ulota-crispa: Small cushions on twigs and branches, leaves crisped when dry, where the air is clean.
tetraphis-pellucida: The only moss with exactly four teeth around its capsule mouth; also spreads from tiny cups.
buxbaumia-aphylla: Barely any leaves: just a big slanted capsule on a stalk, like a bug on a stick.
splachnum-luteum: Grows on moose dung and lures flies with a yellow umbrella and a scent to carry its spores.
schistostega-pennata: Goblin gold: lens-shaped cells catch the faintest light, so it glows in caves and burrows.
hookeria-lucens: Translucent, glistening leaves with cells big enough to see with a hand lens, on wet banks.
calliergonella-cuspidata: Shoots ending in a sharp spear-like tip, in marshes, fens and wet lawns.
racomitrium-lanuginosum: Woolly grey carpets on mountain tops and rocky moors, each leaf ending in a white hair.
physcomitrium-pyriforme: A tiny moss of mud and bare ground, carrying capsules shaped like pears.
aulacomnium-palustre: Yellow-green tufts in bogs and fens, often topped with small balls of buds on a bare stalk.
dicranella-heteromalla: Silky tufts on shady banks, with fine leaves all swept the same way.
pogonatum-urnigerum: A bluish-grey haircap of gravelly banks and tracks, with urn-shaped capsules.
ptilium-crista-castrensis: Regular plume-shaped shoots like ostrich feathers, in old conifer forests.
andreaea-rupestris: Dark red-brown cushions on bare acid rock; its capsule opens by four slits like a lantern.
rhizomnium-punctatum: Round, dark-bordered leaves on reddish stems, beside streams and on wet logs.
bartramia-pomiformis: Round green capsules like tiny apples among soft bluish-green leaves.
encalypta-streptocarpa: Its capsules wear a long hood like a candle snuffer, on chalk and old mortar.
hedwigia-ciliata: Hoary grey mats on sunny rocks, its leaves tipped with white fringed points.
